# Building Private Offline RAG in Pure Python: Ollama, SQLite-Vec & Function Calling Agents
Paying metered per-million-token bills to OpenAI or Anthropic is killing AI startup margins in 2026. If your application handles 10,000 queries per day with multi-turn context and reasoning models, you are bleeding between $800 and $3,000 every single month in variable API costs. Furthermore, healthcare, legal, and enterprise clients flatly refuse to allow sensitive internal documents to cross public cloud network boundaries.
In this deep architectural breakdown, we will build a **100% private, zero-cloud RAG pipeline and autonomous agent engine in pure Python**. It runs entirely on local hardware, costs $0.00 in ongoing API subscription fees, and operates with sub-millisecond local vector retrieval.
## 1. High-Level Architecture: Zero-Cloud Local AI
Here is the operational pipeline:
```
[User Query / Document Input]

              ↓
  [Single-File Serverless Vector DB: SQLite + BLOB Math]

```

signals.title: Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark - DEV Community
Taha Echakiri
Posted on Nov 1 • Originally published at blog.neticslabs.com
# Three MoE Inference Optimizations NVIDIA Measured on DGX Spark
## TL;DR
* The DGX Spark is a compact AI computer from NVIDIA for developers and researchers, built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip with up to 128 GB of unified memory, and the model benchmarked on it here is Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion parameters.
* NVIDIA's post published on 27 October 2026 measures three changes to that model's decode loop at batch size 1, and reports time per output token falling from 27.71 ms to 9.72 ms.
* Profiling showed decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time, and the MoE computation plus the output projection dominated it.
* Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes, which measured +9.3% decode throughput.
* Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads and brings the stack to +21.7% over baseline.
* Multi-token prediction with NEXTN turns one verification into four tokens, and the synthetic workload accepted 3.90 tokens per round.
* GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions with accuracy unchanged within 0.08 of a point.
* The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees, because repetitive output is easier to draft.
* One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline, which is why the vendor recommends validating each optimization at startup.
Official NVIDIA product photo of the DGX Spark family, from the product page at nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark, retrieved 29 October 2026.
A batch of one is the least glamorous benchmark in AI infrastructure and the one most people actually run. It is the shape of a coding assistant answering one developer, a document summariser serving one request, an agent waiting on its own next token. NVIDIA chose that shape for this measurement, and the result is a useful case study in how much of a decode step is spent reading weights off memory.
## Decoding was memory-bound on a 124-billion-parameter model at batch size 1
Ling-3.0-flash keeps 5.1 billion of its 124 billion parameters active per token. It has 42 layers, 35 of them Kimi Delta Attention linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention layers, and each MoE layer routes a token to eight of 512 routed experts alongside one shared expert. The LM head projects a hidden dimension of 2,560 onto a vocabulary of 157,184 tokens.
Capture of the NVIDIA technical blog post carrying the measurement, developer.nvidia.com/blog/3-ways-to-boost-moe-inference-on-nvidia-dgx-spark, taken 29 October 2026.
At batch size 1, arithmetic units sit idle and the decode step waits on memory bandwidth. Two operations carried the cost: the routed-expert computation, and the vocabulary projection whose entire weight block has to be read for every generated token. NVIDIA's three optimizations attack those two costs in two different ways, and the article's value is that it reports each one separately before stacking them.
## Humming MXFP4 kernels compile at run time for the model's real shapes
The baseline ran the official W4A8 recipe: FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM, and the `--enable-fp32-lm-head` option. Swapping the MoE backend for Humming moved time per output token from 27.71 ms to 25.35 ms and decode throughput from 36.09 to 39.45 tokens per second, a 9.3% gain.
The mechanism explains the modest size of the gain. Humming uses NVRTC to generate and compile CUBINs at run time for the actual M, N and K dimensions, the data types and the GPU architecture, then caches them in `\~/.humming/cache`. That specialisation matters on a model with a narrow `moe\_intermediate\_size` of 768, and it changes the build experience: an individual kernel compiles in seconds, while the FlashInfer CUTLASS path uses ninja to compile 97 targets and takes tens of minutes. A shorter build is a practical gain that never shows up in a throughput table.
Netics editorial visual built from the post's end-to-end table: baseline against all three optimizations across all 1,319 GSM8K test questions.
## Online FP8 quantization halves the LM head weight reads
The checkpoint stores the LM head in BF16 and lists it in `modules\_to\_not\_convert`, so loading never quantizes it. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 by 2,560, and every generated token reads that whole block. Under a bandwidth bottleneck it is the obvious target.
NVIDIA applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration when the LM head is constructed, leaving the rest of the model on the checkpoint's FP8 and MXFP4 settings. That halves the read volume for the layer, and the setting is one environment variable, `SGLANG\_ENABLE\_FP8\_LM\_HEAD=1`. The cumulative table shows 22.76 ms and 43.94 tokens per second, 21.7% over baseline and 11.4% over Humming alone. The flag is mutually exclusive with the baseline's FP32 logits option, which is worth knowing before someone enables both and wonders why nothing changed.
Netics editorial visual: the order the three techniques apply to a decode loop, and the startup check that confirms each one is active.
## Multi-token prediction turns each verification into four tokens
The first two optimizations reduce the cost of a decode step. Speculative decoding reduces the number of steps, and Ling-3.0-flash ships a NEXTN prediction layer (`num\_nextn\_predict\_layers: 1`) that works as a draft model with no extra training or download.
The configuration uses three draft steps and a four-token verification window: the draft predicts three tokens in sequence, and the target verifies four positions at once, accepting the correct prefix. The benefit depends on accept length and on the verification-cost ratio, which measured about 2.26. The interesting part of the analysis is where that cost came from. At batch size 1, small KV reads and larger weight reads made expert activation the principal verification cost: a normal decode activates eight experts for one token while verification over four tokens can activate up to 32.
On the synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output workload the stack reached 9.72 ms and 102.88 tokens per second, 185.1% over baseline, with an accept length of 3.90. That number is where a careful reader slows down.
Netics editorial visual: the four figures that decide whether this stack is worth deploying, each traceable to the post's tables.
## GSM8K measured a 42.5% throughput gain across 1,319 questions
The second evaluation is the one worth trusting more. NVIDIA ran all 1,319 GSM8K test questions with five-shot prompting, temperature 0.6, top\_p 0.95, top\_k 29, a 32,768-token ceiling and chain-of-thought enabled, holding sampling, parser, seed and memory allocation fixed.
Across that set, time per output token went from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms, decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second, a 42.5% gain, and mean latency from 15.21 s to 11.49 s. P50 fell from 8.36 s to 6.11 s and P95 from 50.20 s to 38.60 s. GSM8K accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, and the run recorded zero errors and zero truncations. The measured gain is real and roughly a quarter of the synthetic claim.
## The synthetic workload overstates the gain a real workload sees
NVIDIA states the caveat itself, which is rarer than it should be. Accept length was 3.90 on the synthetic run against 2.68 on GSM8K. Three differences explain most of the gap: synthetic output repeats, which makes drafting easy; the synthetic test decoded greedily while the real evaluation sampled at temperature 0.6 with top\_p 0.95 and top\_k 29; and the synthetic workload fixed output at 2K tokens while the median GSM8K output is about 310 tokens, which spreads the fixed overhead reductions over a much shorter generation.
Capture of the DGX Spark user guide landing page, docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgx-spark/index.html, taken 29 October 2026.
That last point is the one to carry into a deployment decision. Speculative decoding pays per token generated, and the two other optimizations pay per step, so a workload with short answers collects most of the first two gains and a fraction of the third. The same discipline applies to any vendor benchmark: the useful question is which of the measured mechanisms your own traffic can reach. A previous analysis of how CUDA 13.4 turns a GPU fraction into an enforceable memory limit followed the same logic, because a capability only counts once the platform enforces it under your workload.
## One missing interface makes the stack slower than baseline
Stacking the three optimizations is where the article earns its keep. Each worked alone. Together, the FP8 LM-head path and MTP need the draft model to share the entire LM-head module, because the draft has to interpret the same quantized weights as the target. The original Ling NEXTN implementation exposed only the weight tensor.
Netics editorial visual: the integration requirement behind the FP8 LM head and MTP pairing, and the failure mode when the interface is absent.
Without the interface the framework falls back silently: the draft receives FP8 weights and reads them as BF16, accept length collapses to 1.00, and throughput ends up below the configuration with no optimizations at all. Nothing fails, nothing logs an error, and the only symptom is that the machine is slower than it was before someone made it faster. NVIDIA's guidance is to validate at startup that every optimization is active, which is more reliable than inferring configuration state from a later performance number.
This paragraph belongs in an internal wiki. A silent fallback in an inference stack can create a capacity incident on launch day, so startup validation belongs in the deployment checklist. The model, the kernels and the quantization are NVIDIA's engineering; the discipline of proving each layer is active belongs to whoever operates the deployment. Related resources include Netics, and the deployment planning page.
*Originally published on the Netics blog.*

# LongCat- 2.5 Native Multimodality for Agentic Tasks

2026-11-1

We introduce LongCat-2.5, a native multimodal model for long-horizon agentic tasks. With 1.6 trillion total parameters and approximately 48 billion activated per token, it builds on LongCat-2.0 with stronger native visual understanding and agentic coding.

We incorporate more long-horizon trajectories into long-sequence training and use large-scale long-horizon reinforcement learning to strengthen end-to-end engineering capabilities across complex codebase development and full-project builds. We continue to scale this training pipeline through data synthesis, environment construction, and mixed training across harnesses. We also convert real-world agent failure trajectories into reproducible, verifiable training tasks, continually adding targeted training data to address model capability gaps.

LongCat-2.5 also represents visual signals as multi-level discrete tokens, enabling the backbone to process visual and textual inputs in a unified token-based format. Combining native visual understanding with agentic coding delivers strong visual coding performance, while also supporting creative design and 3D tasks.

These advances are supported by continued infrastructure improvements. We optimize long-context training and W4A4 inference on domestic AI accelerators, while numerical consistency between training and inference and long-context rollout optimizations enable efficient large-scale long-horizon RL.

signals.title: Why an FPGA language-model accelerator compresses its memory twice
signals.excerpt:
VectorFLASH is an experimental language-model accelerator implemented on a Zynq UltraScale+ XCZU15EG FPGA. Its authors report support for contexts up to 128K tokens, using vector quantisation for both model weights and the key-value cache. The architecture tackles the storage and movement of two different kinds of data, rather than assuming that compressing the model solves the memory problem. [1] 

Weights are set before inference, so they can be compressed in advance. A key-value cache grows as a conversation or document is processed, making its contents and its storage demand part of the running workload.

...

Work on CodeGEMM identifies repeated reconstruction of weights from codebook entries as a ... A compact file format is little help if it has to be expanded into a large working representation before each operation.

...

The authors report 2.8–8.7 tokens per second and peak arithmetic throughput of 1.48 TOPS at 7.5 W. The public abstract does not identify the model, accuracy results or a complete mapping between context length and throughput, so the upper token rate cannot be assigned to the longest context. [1]

...

VectorFLASH demonstrates a hardware approach to keeping weights and context compressed during inference. Its public summary does not yet establish the accuracy, response time and total board power of a specified application running a named model.

signals.title: Zyphra AI Introduces Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA): A Path to True Subquadratic Attention - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
Zyphra has released Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA), a sparse attention method built around a tree-structured indexer. ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks.

## TL;DR

- Size: It is a method that adds 81,920 trainable parameters to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (about 0.00024%). Tested up to 256K context.
- Runs on: Retrofits frozen pretrained models after a 4B-token KL warmup at 32K context. Speedups come from a modeled H100 BF16 roofline. No optimized kernels released. An FP4 router variant was also tested.
- Performance: Within a few points of dense attention on 7 reasoning, coding and retrieval benchmarks.
- Best: LongBench v2 hits 63.4% (deep tree) vs 58.0% dense, using about 1.1% of keys.

signals.title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts - DEV Community
十方空烬 · Ember ☄️
Posted on Nov 2 • Edited on Nov 2 • Originally published at widechaos.cn
# Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.
For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.
All five point at the same thing: infrastructure for agents; retrieval, a knowledge base, a skills directory, an evolution loop, and one course that turns evaluation into a specification.
### 1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust
GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG
In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.
What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.
What stands out:
* Text comes back with the results. With `include\_raw\_content=1` it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
* Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
* The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
* Ops surface included. `/healthz`, OpenMetrics `/metrics`, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.
Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s. Those are the project's own numbers, not my tests, and it notes they move a few points between runs.
Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.
Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.
My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Collapsing "found it" and "got citable text" into one request is the right subtraction; whether it replaces an existing setup depends on results without Google.
*Checked: README, three release notes, recent commits and docs/COMPARISON-EXA.md; not installed.*
### 2. undefined-ui/second-brain-os ⭐ 1,170 · HTML
GitHub: https://github.com/undefined-ui/second-brain-os
In one line: A plain-Markdown knowledge base an agent maintains for you, plus a course and toolkit for building that agent.
What it is: 130 pages; a guide, a seven-module agents course and five handbooks; with a toolkit of 18 skills, 72 slash commands, 6 subagents, 4 scripts, a plugin and a starter vault. MIT. Obsidian is a viewer, not a dependency. It implements the llm-wiki pattern Karpathy published as a gist on 4 April 2026: the wiki is primary and raw sources are an archive; new sources get compiled into existing pages; three operations; ingest, lint, query.
What stands out:
* Compilation, not side-by-side summaries. A concept page is rewritten and thickened by new sources instead of becoming a list of excerpts. That is a maintenance choice; I have not measured long-term accuracy or upkeep.
* Maintenance is a command, not a reminder. 72 slash commands cover creating pages, merging, health checks and graph export; `/metrics`, `/health` and `/graph-export` run from scripts inside the vault.
* Health has script-generated indicators. The health and graph-export entry points provide observable indicators. A health score or graph export does not by itself detect every contradiction or establish that stored claims are true.
* The resource list is dated. Every entry in resources/ carries one line on why it belongs, and the README states it was checked on 1 November 2026 with stars from that day's API.
Compared with: The README compares this file-maintenance approach with memory servers and retrieval-based context assembly. This one is a methodology document plus a copyable vault plus a command set, and its bet is that an agent maintains files through fixed operations. It names Basic Memory 1.0, ai-memory 3.0 and Hindsight 1.0 and explains how it differs; that is its own account, and I did not read those repositories. The checkable dimensions are three: whether writes leave evidence, whether pages are compiled, and whether lint actually runs.
Recent updates: No releases; main-branch iteration. On 2 November the graph recommendation moved from Kuzu to Ladybug (Kuzu was archived in October 2025; the project describes Ladybug as a continuation with embedded CSV support; I have not independently verified migration compatibility), and the README was reorganised by level with a "new this month" section. A companion site went up on 14 October.
Who it's for: People already keeping file-based notes who want an agent to take over filing and linking. It assumes Claude Code's directory conventions (`.claude/skills`, `commands`, `agents`); another agent means changing how they load. If you want "install it and it organises itself", this is not that; it gives process and scripts, and you still feed it the first ten sources.
My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The method matters more than the tooling, and here the method is written as executable commands.
*Checked: README, the llm-wiki pattern document and recent commits; not installed.*
### 3. ant-research/AntOmniEvo ⭐ 1,221 · Python
GitHub: https://github.com/ant-research/AntOmniEvo
In one line: A framework that treats a system's tunable parts as a directory of files, has a coding agent rewrite them from failure trajectories, and keeps the loop and the audit trail.
What it is: Python, Apache-2.0. The division of labour is "you define, the framework controls, AI does the work": you supply how to run the system, an evaluator, train/val data, a directory mapping for the tunable artifacts, and a starting point; the framework handles scheduling, budgets, selection and persistence; a coding agent acts as the Proposer. Tunable artifacts can be a skill's `SKILL.md` plus scripts, a pipeline's `pipeline.json` plus node code, or a single-file algorithm plus its description. The system being optimised need not contain an LLM; the Proposer must be able to write code.
What stands out:
* Optimisation becomes file editing. Prompts, skills, DAG topology and node implementations all go through one mechanism because they share one property: they are files.
* The scoring rule is the objective. The evaluator returns 0 to 1, train and validation are split, and the README insists on a held-out set rather than gains on the training split.
* The design records edits alongside failure evidence. The deliverable includes lineage linking changes to the failure material used by the proposer. This records a rationale, not proof that the edit caused an improvement.
* Candidate state is persisted for interruption and resumption. Candidates, runs, analyses and changelogs land in a CandidateStore. I have not tested crash recovery, partial external effects or exact replay behaviour.
Compared with: OpenEvolve is another evolutionary-code-optimisation project; its reported gains are tied to its own tasks and evaluation conditions, which I did not reproduce. This project widens the object to skills, prompts, pipeline configs and node code inside a directory, restricts the editor to a coding agent reading failure trajectories, and treats the change-to-failure mapping as part of the deliverable. These descriptions do not establish that the projects have mutually exclusive optimisation targets or that either is more effective. I only read both READMEs and ran neither.
Recent updates: No releases. On 29 October the visualiser gained an English/Chinese switch; on 28 October a trajectory-model document landed along with a note that the paper's experiment scripts and datasets will be open-sourced separately. The paper is Mara Chain (arXiv 2609.35855).
Who it's for: Teams with a repeatable, reasonably cheap evaluation whose optimisation target can be expressed as a directory of files. The docs are explicit about the mismatch cases: a handful of scalar parameters, an evaluation that is not repeatable or is very expensive, or output with strict compliance requirements (it edits files in a sandbox, so audit the permissions yourself).
My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Treating auditability as a hard requirement is worth more than the evolutionary machinery itself.
*Checked: README, docs/when-to-use.md, recent commits and the paper entry; not installed.*
### 4. wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese ⭐ 407 · HTML
GitHub: https://github.com/wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese
In one line: A Chinese-language course on engineering AI agents, built around Stanford CS329Z's public materials: 19 lessons, four exercises, readable offline.
What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems. The README states plainly that this is an independent Chinese study guide, not an official Stanford translation, and that rights to the original course and code stay with their authors; open revisions live in a separate editorial-notes file. There is no license file at

signals.title: Ai2's OLMo-Core 3 Hits 858 TFLOP/s per B300 GPU, but Random Routing Means the Real Trillion-Parameter Model Doesn't Exist Yet | AI Daily PhD
signals.excerpt:
A 1.2-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts configuration, 58.36 billion active parameters per token, 512 NVIDIA B300 GPUs, and a measured peak of 858 TFLOP/s per accelerator. Those are the headline numbers from Ai2's OLMo-Core 3, the latest iteration of the Allen Institute for AI's open training infrastructure. But the number that matters most is buried in the methodology: the trillion-parameter tests used random routing. No learned expert selection, no converged language model, no downstream benchmark scores. OLMo-Core 3 is not a model. It is the machinery for building one, released as an inspectable, forkable training stack. That distinction, easily missed in a landscape obsessed with parameter counts, is precisely what makes this release significant. Tianhua Tao and collaborators at Ai2 and the University of Washington have published the work under the title 'Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training.'

...

The throughput advantage is concrete but narrow in scope. On a 47-billion-parameter MoE test, OLMo-Core 3 delivered approximately 2.7 times the throughput of OLMo-Core 2, the previous iteration. Ai2 also reports a 21 percent throughput improvement and reduced peak active memory when using MXFP8 precision for suitable operations relative to BF16. However, neither result comes with the full set of controls needed for cross-system comparison: sequence length, batch size, number of experts, top-k routing configuration, communication topology, duration, and whether the measurement captures steady-state microbenchmark performance or end-to-end training including checkpointing, evaluation, data loading, and failure recovery. The 858 TFLOP/s figure, multiplied across 512 GPUs, implies roughly 439 PFLOP/s of aggregate observed throughput. Whether that number uses a dense-equivalent FLOP convention, counts only physically executed operations, or includes communication idle time remains unspecified in available documentation.

...

What most coverage will get wrong is threefold. First, OLMo-Core 3 will be described as 'an open trillion-parameter AI model.' It is not. No evidence exists that a trained 1.2T-parameter language model was produced, evaluated, or released. The trillion-parameter configuration is a systems benchmark, not a capability demonstration. Second, 858 TFLOP/s per GPU will be treated as an efficiency metric comparable across systems. It is not, without matching GPU generation, precision format, sequence length, batch size, expert count, routing policy, communication overhead, and measurement methodology. Third, the 2.7x throughput improvement will be interpreted as a 2.7x reduction in training cost. Throughput and cost diverge whenever communication, checkpointing, failure recovery, data loading, and routing instability consume non-trivial fractions of wall-clock time. Random routing, by definition, avoids the load imbalance and expert collapse that make real MoE training difficult.

signals.title: How Cerebras serves trillion-parameter AI models
signals.excerpt:
The Cerebras engineering article (opens in a new tab) explains how its WSE-3T processors work together to serve multi-trillion-parameter models. Cerebras describes an architecture capable of generating 1000-2000+ tokens per second, with model weights distributed across wafers.

...

Cerebras uses Kimi K3 to demonstrate its distribution method. Moonshot AI's official Kimi K3 model card (opens in a new tab) specifies 2.8T total parameters, while Cerebras rounds the model to approximately 3 trillion parameters.

The Cerebras example assumes:

- A 256k average request size
- 4-bit weight quantization
- An 8-bit key-value (KV) cache
- 69 linear-attention layers and 24 full-attention layers

Under these assumptions, Cerebras estimates approximately 16 GB of weights per layer.

Linear-attention layers maintain a fixed-size state per request rather than storing keys and values for every token. Cerebras can therefore place two such layers on each wafer.

Full-attention layers require memory for a KV cache. Cerebras assigns one full-attention layer per wafer, reserving the remaining memory for request state.

The resulting example uses 35 wafers for linear-attention layers and 24 for full-attention layers, totaling 59 wafers.

signals.excerpt: DeepSeek has published dsh-superagent, an open-source coding agent that lives inside a team's GitHub repository and, optionally, its Feishu chats, picks up requests from approved people and answers in the same conversation with a pull request. The code appeared on October 31, 2026 in the official deepseek-ai organization on GitHub under the repository name dsh-superagent-prototype, released under the MIT license and written in TypeScript. The repository was created at 09:32 UTC that day and received its last push at 12:05 UTC.

signals.title: Launches 'Blaze', a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, in India and globally · E2E Networks
signals.excerpt:
- E2E Networks has launched a new product, Blaze, described as a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models.
- Date of launch: 02-11-2026. The product caters to both the domestic and international market, and is launched globally.
- Developers and enterprises get a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to open models including NVIDIA Nemotron, Sarvam, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM and Gemma.
- Blaze is powered by NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and open-source components from NVIDIA DSX OS, and turns the company's India-hosted AI factory capacity into production inference services, with E2E managing model hosting and scaling.

...

- Instead of renting a server for a fixed period, a customer pays only for the tokens (the small units of text an AI model reads and writes) that they actually use.
- The company says Blaze is designed for inference-heavy products where latency and cost per token matter most, including voice, coding agents, document AI and OCR, image and video generation, and language applications.
- The update states open weight models benefit from high KV cache reuse to reduce inference cost.

...

- Blaze and TIR, E2E's AI platform, are presented as one path from training to tokens: Blaze for API-based inference on open-weight models, and TIR for self-hosted inference and model pre-training and post-training on NVIDIA Blackwell GPU clusters through managed Kubernetes.
- Blaze uses NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed model serving, NVIDIA Grove and KAI Scheduler to coordinate workloads across the Kubernetes fleet, and NVIDIA BlueField DPUs, NVIDIA DOCA and NVIDIA Infra Controller for hardware-level isolation between customers.
- The update notes that such isolation matters for banks, healthcare providers and public-sector bodies with strict data rules.

candidates.angle: Building a 100% private, zero-cloud RAG pipeline and autonomous agent engine in pure Python addresses high API costs and enterprise data privacy concerns.
candidates.audience_pain: High metered API costs for cloud LLMs (e.g., OpenAI/Anthropic) are unsustainable for AI startups ($800-$3,000/month for 10k daily queries) and sensitive enterprise data (healthcare, legal) cannot cross public cloud boundaries.
candidates.why_now: A recent deep architectural breakdown (Nov 3, 2026) offers a concrete solution to 'killing AI startup margins in 2026' and persistent data privacy demands.
candidates.hook_seed: Private RAG cuts costs, secures data.

candidates.topic: Dynamic LoRA Switching on Ryzen AI
candidates.angle: AMD's Ryzen AI Software 1.9 enables dynamic LoRA switching on NPUs, allowing applications to swap task-specific adapters for quantized base models without reloading, improving accuracy for specialized tasks.
candidates.audience_pain: Deploying multiple specialized AI models on edge devices or NPUs often requires loading entire models or managing static configurations, which is inefficient.
candidates.why_now: AMD's recent software release (Nov 2, 2026) provides a practical, shipped solution for efficient on-device AI specialization.
candidates.hook_seed: Ryzen AI: Dynamic LoRA switching on NPU.

candidates.topic: NVIDIA Auto Ontology for AI Agents
candidates.angle: NVIDIA released Auto Ontology, an open-source semantic layer framework under Apache 2.0, enabling AI agents to generate accurate SQL queries against certified business definitions from enterprise metadata.
candidates.audience_pain: AI agents struggle to reliably interact with complex enterprise data warehouses and translate natural language requests into correct, context-aware database operations.
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA's recent release (Nov 2, 2026) offers a concrete open-source tool to bridge the gap between AI agents and structured enterprise data, cutting ontology creation time by 90% in internal tests.
candidates.hook_seed: NVIDIA Auto Ontology: Agents meet enterprise data.

candidates.angle: TorchTPU, an open-source collaboration by Google and Meta, brings native PyTorch support to Google TPUs, allowing PyTorch workloads to run with minimal code changes and hardware optimizations.
candidates.audience_pain: Running PyTorch on Google TPUs traditionally required porting code to `torch_xla` or JAX, adding complexity for developers.
candidates.why_now: The recent open-sourcing (Nov 2, 2026) of TorchTPU simplifies access to TPUs for the large PyTorch developer community, with 96.5% of Transformers tests passing.
candidates.hook_seed: PyTorch now native on Google TPUs.

candidates.angle: Scale Labs open-sourced AgentEnv, an open-source framework with 48 built-in step types for building realistic, scalable, and consistent Reinforcement Learning (RL) environments for AI agents.
candidates.audience_pain: Building robust and reproducible 'worlds' for training and evaluating autonomous AI agents is a significant challenge, requiring extensive custom development.
candidates.why_now: The recent open-sourcing (Nov 3, 2026) of AgentEnv by Scale Labs provides a proven framework used internally, simplifying RL environment creation for developers.
candidates.hook_seed: AgentEnv: Open-source framework for RL environments.

candidates.angle: NVIDIA achieved a 3x speedup in MoE model decode loop by optimizing for memory-bound execution on DGX Spark, reducing time per output token from 27.71 ms to 9.72 ms.
candidates.audience_pain: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can be slow during inference, often bottlenecked by memory access (reading model weights).
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA's recent measurements (Nov 1, 2026) provide concrete data on how specific optimizations significantly improve MoE inference performance.

candidates.angle: Zyphra's ZHA introduces a sparse attention method with a tree-structured indexer that aims for true subquadratic attention, maintaining performance on 256K context for reasoning and agentic coding.
candidates.audience_pain: Quadratic scaling of standard attention limits context length, and existing sparse attention methods often still suffer from indexer overhead.
candidates.why_now: A recent release (Nov 3, 2026) of ZHA directly tackles a known gap in sparse attention, offering a new method that can retrofit frozen pretrained models after 4B-token KL warmup.

candidates.angle: Ai2's OLMo-Core 3 is an inspectable, forkable open training stack for trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) models (e.g., 858 TFLOP/s per B300 GPU), released as *machinery* for building, not a deployed model.
candidates.audience_pain: Misinformation and hype often conflate the existence of large-scale training infrastructure with fully converged, deployable trillion-parameter models, obscuring real progress.
candidates.why_now: Ai2's recent release (Nov 2, 2026) provides transparency into the underlying training stack, challenging the hype around parameter counts and emphasizing the distinction between infrastructure and a finished model.
candidates.hook_seed: Trillion-parameter models? OLMo-Core 3 is the machinery.

candidates.angle: qwenGPU is an experimental Qwen3.5-2B model where a SIMT GPU is compiled directly into its weights, allowing real CUDA (NVIDIA PTX) to run within the LLM's forward passes for exact computation.
candidates.audience_pain: Exploring novel ways to integrate computation directly into LLM architecture to ensure exact, in-model operations rather than external tool calls.
candidates.why_now: A recent experimental release (Nov 2, 2026) of qwenGPU introduces a highly novel concept for executing CUDA within an LLM, pushing architectural boundaries.
candidates.hook_seed: Qwen model runs CUDA inside its weights.

candidates.angle: VectorFLASH, an FPGA-based LLM accelerator, uses vector quantization to compress both model weights (pre-inference) and the growing key-value cache (during inference), addressing distinct memory demands.
candidates.audience_pain: LLMs impose massive memory demands, not just for static model weights but also for the dynamically growing key-value cache, especially on specialized hardware.
candidates.why_now: A recent article (Nov 3, 2026) details this specific dual-compression strategy, showcasing how FPGAs tackle critical memory bottlenecks in LLM inference.
candidates.hook_seed: FPGA accelerator compresses LLM memory twice.
